name: Varanasi
tagline: India's eternal city of light upon the Ganges.
bestMonths: Jan, Feb, Mar, Nov and Dec
whenBlurb: October to March gives cool, clear days along the ghats, with November's Dev Deepawali the most spectacular night of all; avoid the punishing summer and the monsoon floods.

ourTake.lede: Varanasi is India at its most intense and sacred, and it asks you to slow down, take a boat on the Ganga at dawn as the ghats wake, and again at dusk for the Ganga Aarti at Dashashwamedh. Watch the aarti from a boat on the water rather than the packed steps. Walk the old lanes with a guide; getting lost here is not romantic, it's disorienting. Come with respect, not a camera aimed at the cremation ghats.
ourTake.comeIf: You want the Ganges at dawn and one of the oldest living cities on earth.
ourTake.skipIf: You are unsettled by crowds, intensity or open displays of ritual and death.

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes, grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Taj Nadesar Palace
credentials: Taj Hotels / IHCL, heritage palace (built 1782)
Once the residence of the Maharaja of Benares; furnished with the royal family's own pieces
items.description: A 1782 palace of just ten rooms set in mango orchards and rose gardens, the most refined address in the holy city.

items.name: BrijRama Palace, Varanasi, By the Ganges
credentials: Brij Hotels, heritage palace (built 1812), the second-oldest palace in Varanasi
Riverfront heritage on Darbhanga Ghat; India's first heritage lift
items.description: An 1812 palace rising straight from Darbhanga Ghat, the city's finest riverfront heritage address, the Ganga at your feet.

items.name: Taj Ganges, Varanasi
credentials: Taj Hotels / IHCL, official property
Set within a 42-acre garden estate; home to the rooftop pure-veg restaurant Narmada
items.description: A capable, gracious Taj house across 42 acres of gardens, the reliable full-service base near the old city.

items.name: Guleria Kothi at Ganges
credentials: Recognised boutique heritage hotel, 18th-century riverfront kothi
Restored in local sandstone with stone columns and beams, honouring Varanasi's ghat architecture
items.description: An 18th-century riverfront kothi restored in local sandstone, a boutique heritage house on the ghats themselves.

items.name: Ramada by Wyndham Varanasi
credentials: Wyndham Hotels, official Ramada by Wyndham property
Set in a historic district, near Assi Ghat, with an outdoor pool
items.description: A polished, dependable modern hotel minutes from Assi Ghat, the well-run contemporary option in a heritage city.

items.name: A Dawn Boat Ride on the Ganga
items.description: The single defining Banaras experience, push off in the dark from your ghat and let the river carry you south as the sun lifts pink over the far bank and eighty-odd ghats wake at once: pilgrims chest-deep in the water, brass lotas catching the first light, priests under their palm-leaf umbrellas. Ask your hotel for a private wooden bajra with its own oarsman and a Sanskrit-literate guide, and go early enough that the whole crescent is still yours; the light between 5.30 and 7 is the reason people cross the country for this.

items.name: The Ganga Aarti at Dashashwamedh Ghat
items.description: Every evening at dusk, young priests in matching kurtas raise towering multi-tiered brass lamps in perfect synchrony to conch and cymbal and drum, the most theatrical fire ceremony in India, performed at the ghat where Brahma is said to have offered ten horses. The bank fills with thousands; the only civilised vantage is a private boat moored a few metres off the steps, floating a diya of your own on the current while the flames swing above the water. Your concierge arranges the boat and a guide to read the ritual for you.

items.name: The Kashi Vishwanath Temple
credentials: One of the twelve Jyotirlingas of Shiva
items.description: The holiest shrine to Shiva as Lord of the Universe, the golden-spired temple rebuilt by Ahilyabai Holkar in 1780, its dome plated in gold gifted by Maharaja Ranjit Singh. To touch the jyotirlinga here is, for many Hindus, the culmination of a lifetime's pilgrimage. Queues are immense; arrange a sanctum darshan or the early Mangala Aarti through the temple trust so an elder or a multi-generation family reaches the linga with dignity rather than in a crush.

items.name: The Kashi Vishwanath Corridor (Dham)
items.description: The vast stone plaza inaugurated in December 2021 that finally opened the temple to the river, a five-lakh-square-foot sweep of Chunar sandstone connecting Kashi Vishwanath directly to Lalita Ghat on the Ganga, with more than forty centuries-old shrines rediscovered and restored in the clearing of the old lanes. Walk it at dusk from the ghat up to the temple: the scale, the ghat-facing façades and the light on the sandstone are genuinely moving. A guide explains what stood here before.

items.name: Assi Ghat & Subah-e-Banaras
items.description: The southernmost great ghat, at the confluence of the Assi stream and the Ganga, and the calmest place to meet the city at dawn. The daily Subah-e-Banaras programme, begun in 2014, opens at first light with a Vedic havan and sunrise aarti, then a half-hour of live raga and open yoga on the steps, a serene, uncrowded counterpoint to the evening spectacle downstream. Come with your own mat and a flask of chai from a stall; it is free, and it is lovely.

items.name: Manikarnika Ghat
items.description: The great cremation ghat, burning without pause for centuries, where Hindus believe that dying and being cremated in Kashi grants moksha, release from the cycle of rebirth. It is not a spectacle but a threshold, one of the most sacred places in the Hindu world, and it asks for stillness and respect. Photography of the pyres is forbidden; go quietly with a guide who can explain the rites, and never engage the touts who solicit 'donations for wood'.

items.name: Harishchandra Ghat
items.description: The second, older cremation ghat, named for the legendary king Harishchandra who is said to have served here as a keeper of the burning grounds to honour a vow of truth. Smaller and less visited than Manikarnika, it carries the same profound weight of the city's relationship with death as liberation. Approach it with the same reverence and restraint, observe from the river or the upper steps, do not photograph the pyres.

items.name: Panchganga Ghat & the Alamgir Mosque
items.description: The ghat where five sacred rivers are believed to meet, crowned by Aurangzeb's 17th-century Alamgir Mosque rising on the foundations of an older Vishnu temple, the single most photographed silhouette on the northern river-front and a quiet emblem of the city's layered history. Rows of small niche-shrines line the water where devotees light hundreds of lamps at Kartik Purnima. It is a contemplative stop on a slow morning row upriver.

items.name: Kedar Ghat & the Kedareshwar Temple
items.description: The vividly painted ghat, red-and-white striped steps climbing to the Kedareshwar temple, whose Shiva is linked to Kedarnath in the Himalaya and especially revered by South Indian and Bengali pilgrims. Less trafficked than Dashashwamedh, it has an early-morning intimacy: bathers, a warren of shrine lanes above, and a naturally spring-fed tank nearby. A rewarding, colourful pause on a walking route between the central ghats.

items.name: Man Mandir Ghat & the Man Singh Observatory (Jantar Mantar)
items.description: The palace-ghat built in 1585 by Raja Man Singh of Amber, its stone balconies among the finest Rajput carving on the river, crowned by the rooftop Jantar Mantar, the masonry astronomical instruments added by Sawai Jai Singh II around 1710 to track the sun, stars and eclipses. Climb to the terrace for the sight-lines the astronomers used and one of the best elevated views of the ghats. A small ticketed monument, well worth the detour with a guide.

items.name: The Sankat Mochan Hanuman Temple
items.description: One of the most beloved temples in Varanasi, dedicated to Hanuman as the 'reliever of troubles' and founded, by tradition, by the poet-saint Tulsidas on the spot where he had a vision. Set in leafy grounds near the Assi, it is warm, unpretentious and thick with the scent of marigold and besan laddoo prasad. Tuesdays and Saturdays draw devoted crowds; a weekday morning is serene. It also hosts the celebrated Sankat Mochan Sangeet Samaroh music festival.

items.name: The Durga Temple (Monkey Temple)
items.description: The striking 18th-century temple built by a Bengali maharani, painted deep ochre-red and topped with the multi-tiered nagara spire, beside a stepped tank, dedicated to Durga and famous for the troops of resident macaques that give it its nickname. Non-Hindus can admire the architecture and the tank from outside the sanctum. Pair it with the neighbouring Tulsi Manas and Durgakund for a compact southern-city temple circuit; mind bags and spectacles around the monkeys.

items.name: The Tulsi Manas Temple
items.description: A serene white-marble modern temple built in 1964 on the spot where Tulsidas is said to have composed the Ramcharitmanas, his Awadhi retelling of the Ramayana, whose verses are inscribed across the interior walls. Calm, uncrowded and welcoming to all, with gardens and a gentle devotional atmosphere. A gentle, contemplative stop that sets the poet's epic against the temple's cool marble; lovely with grandparents.

items.name: The New Vishwanath Temple at BHU (Birla Temple)
items.description: The soaring white shikhara temple within the green campus of Banaras Hindu University, built by the Birla family to Pandit Malaviya's vision and completed in 1966, modelled on the original Kashi Vishwanath and open to people of every faith, unlike the old shrine. At over seventy metres it is among the tallest temple towers in India, and the calm, spacious grounds are a relief after the density of the old city. Combine with Bharat Kala Bhavan on a half-day BHU visit.

items.name: The Bharat Kala Bhavan Museum
items.description: One of India's finest university museums, founded in 1920 on the BHU campus, more than 100,000 objects spanning Mughal miniatures, Company paintings, Gupta and Kushana sculpture, brocade textiles and archaeology, with the celebrated Krishna and Nidhivan miniature series among the highlights. Quiet, air-cooled and gloriously under-visited; a private guided hour here is one of the most rewarding cultural stops in the city. Photography inside is restricted.

items.name: Ramnagar Fort & Museum
items.description: The 18th-century sandstone fortress-palace of the Kashi Naresh, the maharajas of Banaras, standing across the river on the eastern bank, a rambling seat of Mughal-influenced arches and river-facing balconies whose Saraswati Bhawan museum keeps vintage cars, palanquins, ivory work, arms and an astronomical clock. Cross by boat at golden hour for the approach, or by the Ramnagar bridge. It is also the great stage of the Ramnagar Ramlila each autumn.

items.name: The Ramnagar Ramlila
credentials: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity (as part of Ramlila traditions)
items.description: A month-long, open-air enactment of the Ramayana staged across the town and grounds of Ramnagar each autumn since the 19th century, the audience walks with the play from site to site, and the Kashi Naresh traditionally rides out on an elephant to open the great episodes. It is theatre, pilgrimage and community ritual at once, unlike anything else in India. If your dates align around Dussehra, a guide who knows the nightly sequence is essential.

items.name: A Heritage Walk Through the Old-City Galis
items.description: The true Banaras is not on the river but in the labyrinth behind it, a maze of galis too narrow for cars, lined with shrines every few steps, wrestling akharas, brass-workers, sweet stalls and hidden courtyards, where a wandering bull may bring the lane to a standstill. It is easy to get pleasantly lost and hard to read without help; a knowledgeable local guide turns the confusion into the richest few hours in the city. Best at dawn, before the crush.

items.name: Vishwanath Gali & the Temple Bazaar
items.description: The dense, dazzling lane leading to the Kashi Vishwanath temple, lined shoulder-to-shoulder with stalls of rudraksha malas, brass and copper puja ware, sindoor, incense, silver and heaps of marigold, the sensory overture to the shrine. It is chaotic and wonderful; a guide steers you past the touts to the genuine brass-workers and the good sweet shops. Come for the atmosphere and the small ritual purchases as much as the shopping.

items.name: The Banarasi Silk Weavers of Madanpura
credentials: Banarasi sari, Geographical Indication (GI) protected
items.description: The old weaving mohalla where families have worked the handloom for generations, the clack of the pit-loom behind every doorway, silk shot with real gold and silver zari into the kalga, jaal and butta motifs that define the Banarasi sari. A pre-arranged visit to a reputable weaver's home lets you watch a master at the loom and choose brocade at source rather than in a showroom. Insist on genuine handloom; ask your concierge for a vetted introduction.

items.name: Thandai & Paan in the Old City
items.description: Two Banarasi rituals no visit is complete without, the cool, spiced almond-and-saffron thandai served in kulhads at legendary shops like Blue Lassi and the old thandai houses, and the celebrated Banarasi paan, the folded betel leaf that the city treats as an art form and a farewell. Have your guide take you to the trusted, hygienic institutions; the classic paan is a fragrant sweet meetha, not the tobacco-laced kind.

items.name: The Bharat Mata Temple
items.description: A temple like no other, inaugurated by Mahatma Gandhi in 1936, it enshrines not a deity but a vast relief map of undivided India carved in marble, its mountains, rivers and plains rendered to scale. Built by the nationalist Babu Shiv Prasad Gupta, it is a quietly moving monument to the idea of the nation rather than a place of worship. A short, unusual and thought-provoking stop, especially with older children.

items.name: The Nepali Temple (Kathwala) at Lalita Ghat
items.description: A hidden 19th-century gem, a fragrant terracotta-and-timber temple built by a king of Nepal as a small replica of Kathmandu's Pashupatinath, its dark wood intricately carved in true Nepali style and set among trees above the ghat. Peaceful and easily missed, it rewards the traveller who goes looking. A short climb from Lalita Ghat, now beside the Vishwanath Corridor; a serene ten minutes away from the crowds.

items.name: Chausatthi Ghat & the Chausatthi Devi Temple
items.description: A quieter, atmospheric ghat rebuilt by the rulers of Udaipur, climbing steeply to the small shrine of the sixty-four yoginis, the chausatth devis for whom it is named. It has a gentle, lived-in intimacy and fine morning light for photography without the crowds of Dashashwamedh a few steps north. A hidden pause on a slow riverside walk between the central ghats.

items.name: The Banaras Gharana & a Private Classical Music Evening
credentials: Varanasi, UNESCO Creative City of Music
items.description: Varanasi is a UNESCO Creative City of Music and the seat of the Banaras gharana, the lineage of Bismillah Khan's shehnai, of tabla, thumri and dhrupad that has shaped Hindustani classical music for centuries. Through your concierge you can sit in a private baithak in a musician's own haveli, a handful of guests before a master of sitar or tabla, the most intimate and authentic way to hear the city's other great inheritance. Book ahead; the finest artists play by arrangement.

items.name: The Sankat Mochan Sangeet Samaroh
items.description: The city's revered classical music and dance festival, held each spring in the courtyard of the Sankat Mochan temple around Hanuman Jayanti, where India's greatest musicians perform through the night for free, taking no fee, as an offering to Hanuman. Unpretentious, all-night and genuinely sacred rather than commercial, it is a pilgrimage in its own right for music lovers. If your visit coincides, a guide secures a good place among the mats.

items.name: Sarnath, The Dhamek Stupa & the Deer Park
credentials: Ancient Buddhist Site, Sarnath, UNESCO World Heritage Tentative List (nominated 2025)
items.description: The gentle, green counterpoint to Kashi's intensity, the Deer Park where the Buddha gave his first sermon and set the Wheel of Dharma turning, one of the four holiest sites in Buddhism. At its heart the massive Gupta-era Dhamek Stupa rises above the excavated monastery ruins and the stump of Ashoka's pillar. A half-day trip of great calm; walk the ruins slowly with a guide who can trace the story of that first teaching.

items.name: The Archaeological Museum, Sarnath
credentials: Home of the original Lion Capital of Ashoka, India's national emblem
items.description: The oldest site museum of the Archaeological Survey of India, opened in 1910, and the home of the original Lion Capital of Ashoka, the four back-to-back lions carved around 250 BCE that India adopted as its national emblem. To stand before the actual stone that every rupee and passport reproduces is quietly electrifying. Small, superb and unmissable on any Sarnath visit; combine with the stupa across the road.

items.name: The Mulagandha Kuti Vihar & Bodhi Tree, Sarnath
items.description: The 1931 Mahabodhi Society temple beside the ruins, its interior lined with Kosetsu Nosu's celebrated frescoes of the Buddha's life and enshrining relics, set beside a sapling of the Bodh Gaya Bodhi tree, itself grown from the original tree at Anuradhapura. The surrounding gardens hold monasteries built by Thailand, Tibet, Japan, China and Sri Lanka, giving a living, international sense of the Buddhist world. A peaceful, meditative complement to the ancient stupa.

items.name: The Tibetan & Buddhist Monasteries of Sarnath
items.description: Around the ancient ruins Sarnath has become a quiet living centre of world Buddhism, the Tibetan temple with its great prayer wheel, the Wat Thai Sarnath with its towering standing Buddha, and Chinese, Japanese and Burmese monasteries, many with resident monks and gardens open to visitors. A gentle wander among them shows how the Buddha's first teaching still gathers the whole of Asia to this one field. Modest dress and quiet observance are appreciated.

items.name: Chunar Fort
items.description: A dramatic sandstone fortress on a rocky bluff above a bend of the Ganga, its history running through the Mughals, Sher Shah Suri and the British, a windswept, atmospheric day-trip upriver with sweeping views over the river and the old town famous for its sandstone quarries and pottery. Far quieter than the Varanasi sites; a car and a guide make an easy morning of it, ideally combined with the drive along the Ganga.

items.name: The Ganga Aarti by Private Boat at Assi Ghat
items.description: The evening aarti at Assi is smaller and gentler than the great ceremony at Dashashwamedh, and for many families the more moving for it, the lamps swung against the dusk with the southern ghats emptier and calmer around you. Watch it from your own boat moored a few metres off the steps, cool river air, your own diyas on the water, an unhurried counterpoint to the downstream crowds. Your concierge arranges the boat and timing.

items.name: Meander Ghat to Ghat on Foot at First Light
items.description: Between Assi in the south and Raj Ghat in the north run more than eighty ghats, each with its own name, shrine and character, Munshi, Darbhanga, Chausatthi, Meer, Scindia with its half-sunken temple, the wrestlers' akharas, the dhobi ghats and the palaces of vanished princes. Walking the crescent slowly at dawn, before the boats fill, is the most rewarding free thing to do in Banaras. A guide reads the ghats like a book of the city's history.

items.name: The Kal Bhairav Temple
items.description: The fierce guardian-deity of Kashi, Bhairava, the terrifying form of Shiva who is believed to be the kotwal, the police chief, of the sacred city; tradition holds that no pilgrimage to Varanasi is complete without his darshan. A vivid, intense little temple in the northern old city, garlanded and thick with devotees, where the priests tie a black protective thread on the wrist. Off the tourist trail and all the more authentic for it; a guide finds it in the lanes.

items.name: The Annapurna Devi Temple
items.description: Beside Kashi Vishwanath stands the temple of Annapurna, the goddess of nourishment and Shiva's consort as the one who feeds the city, in Kashi's mythology it is she who ensures no one in the sacred city goes hungry. Warm and devotional, it is a natural companion to the great Shiva temple next door, and its golden Annapurna is shown to the public only around Dhanteras. A meaningful, easily-added stop within the corridor precinct.

items.name: The Sarnath Light-and-Sound Show
items.description: In the evenings the excavated ruins around the Dhamek Stupa become the screen for a son-et-lumière that narrates the Buddha's journey to Sarnath and the birth of his teaching, the old brick monasteries lit against the dark. It is an atmospheric, unhurried way to end a Sarnath day and gives children and grandparents the story in a single sitting. Check current timings and weather; your concierge confirms the schedule.

items.name: The Ropeway over the Ganga & Old City
items.description: Varanasi's new urban ropeway, among the first passenger cable-cars of its kind in India, lifts you in glass cabins high above the tangled old city and the river, a startling new way to grasp the geography of the ghats and the corridor from the air. A quick, novel and family-friendly ride that reframes everything you have walked below. A modern curiosity rather than a pilgrimage, but a genuinely good vantage on a busy city.

items.name: The Vishwanath Temple Mangala Aarti at Dawn
items.description: Long before sunrise the day at Kashi Vishwanath begins with the Mangala Aarti, the first waking of the deity in the small hours, in a near-empty sanctum, by lamp and bell, before the pilgrim tide arrives. A limited number of passes are issued daily; secured in advance through the temple trust, it is the most intimate and unhurried darshan possible at the holiest of Shiva shrines. Your concierge arranges the pass and the pre-dawn transfer.

items.name: Silk & Brocade at a Trusted Banarasi House
credentials: Banarasi sari, Geographical Indication (GI) protected
items.description: For a bridal Banarasi or an heirloom brocade, the answer is not a tourist showroom but an introduction to one of the established weaving houses, where you see the handloom, understand real zari from imitation, and commission a piece to your own design. A vetted, no-pressure visit arranged by your concierge is the difference between a genuine handwoven treasure and a machine-made copy. Ask specifically to see katan silk and the family's own looms.

items.name: The Trilochan & Northern Ghats
items.description: At the quiet northern end of the crescent, Trilochan, 'three-eyed', for Shiva, is one of the city's oldest and most sacred ghats, its twin turreted shrines rising from the water and its bathing believed especially auspicious. Far from the visitor circuit, it shows the working, devotional river without any performance for outsiders. A rewarding stop on a longer upriver row, best reached by boat with a guide who knows the old northern shrines.

items.name: A Sattvic Cooking or Puja Experience in a Banaras Home
items.description: Beyond the temples, the city's pure-vegetarian, sattvic kitchen is its own tradition, the kachoris and jalebis of the morning, the chaats, the malaiyo winter foam, all meat-free by the sacredness of the ground. A private session in a Brahmin household, a home puja, a hands-on Banarasi vegetarian lesson, gives a multi-generation family the city's living culture rather than only its monuments. Arranged discreetly through your concierge with a vetted host.

items.name: Sunset from the Water off Chet Singh Ghat
items.description: The fortified riverside palace of the 18th-century Raja Chet Singh, who defied the British East India Company, rises straight from the water in the southern stretch of ghats, best seen not from the steps but from a boat as the sun drops behind the city and the sandstone turns amber. A serene, uncrowded golden-hour drift, away from the aarti crowds, with the old princely façades lit along the bank. Pair it with an early evening row.

items.name: The Vyasa Temple & Ghats at Ramnagar
items.description: The eastern bank at Ramnagar has its own quieter riverfront and the shrine of Vyasa, compiler of the Vedas, who is said by legend to have been made to live across the river from Kashi proper. Combined with the fort, it makes the far bank a calm half-day away from the intensity of the main ghats, with long views back across the Ganga to the city's whole crescent. Reach it by boat for the best perspective on Banaras itself.

items.name: Narmada, Taj Ganges
credentials: Inside Taj Ganges, Taj Hotels / IHCL
Rooftop pure-vegetarian restaurant
items.description: Pure-vegetarian dining on the Taj Ganges rooftop, the horizon opening toward the river, the city's most refined veg table.

items.name: Dining at Taj Nadesar Palace
credentials: Inside Taj Nadesar Palace, Taj Hotels / IHCL heritage palace (1782)
items.description: Royal-kitchen cooking in a 1782 palace of ten rooms, modern Indian and global dishes touched with Benares history.

items.name: Dining at BrijRama Palace
credentials: Inside BrijRama Palace, Brij Hotels heritage palace (1812)
Rooftop / riverfront dining on Darbhanga Ghat
items.description: Pure-vegetarian cooking above the Ganga at Darbhanga Ghat, dinner with the river and the aarti below.

items.name: Kashi Chat Bhandar
credentials: Legendary Banarasi chaat institution, c. 70 years
A fixture of Varanasi street-food culture, Godowlia
items.description: Seven decades of Banaras chaat, tamatar chaat and palak chaat that regulars will tell you define the city.

items.name: Blue Lassi Shop
credentials: Legendary lassi institution, three generations
A Kachori Gali fixture, widely featured in travel press
items.description: Three generations of thick, malai-topped lassi in a tiny lane near the ghats, a Banaras rite of passage.

items.name: Baati Chokha
credentials: Recognised local heritage restaurant for authentic Bhojpuri-Banarasi cuisine
Traditional village-style dining, charpoys, folk art, leaf plates
items.description: Rustic Bhojpuri-Banarasi cooking, litti-chokha and baati in ghee, served village-style on leaf plates.

items.name: Deena Chaat Bhandar
credentials: Legendary Banarasi chaat institution, c. 50 years
A long-standing fixture of Varanasi's street-food culture
items.description: A half-century of Banaras chaat, the local counterpoint to Kashi Chat, and every bit as loved.

items.name: The evening Ganga Aarti
credentials: Varanasi's true evening event, the nightly Ganga Aarti at Dashashwamedh Ghat
The city is a place of pilgrimage and sobriety; this is the occasion, not a bar
items.description: In a spiritual, largely dry city, the night belongs to the river, fire, drums and prayer at the water's edge, watched from a boat.

items.name: Rooftop dining over the Ganga, BrijRama & Guleria Kothi
credentials: Heritage-hotel riverfront rooftops, BrijRama Palace (1812) and Guleria Kothi
Honest to the city: an evening of the river, not a cocktail scene
items.description: The city's after-dark grace note, a quiet rooftop above the river, the aarti glowing on the ghats below.

plan.heading: 3 days in Varanasi, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip, the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Settle at the Taj Nadesar Palace or BrijRama Palace on the ghats, then rest before the evening.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A late-afternoon walk through the old lanes to the Kashi Vishwanath corridor with a scholar-guide.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A private boat for the Ganga Aarti at Dashashwamedh Ghat, watching the ritual from the water at a respectful distance.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A dawn rowboat along the ghats as the city bathes and prays, ending with breakfast at Assi Ghat.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Drive to Sarnath, where the Buddha gave his first sermon, walking the Dhamek Stupa and museum in quiet.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A classical sitar or dhrupad recital arranged privately, then dinner at the hotel.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A morning with a master Banarasi silk weaver in the Muslim weavers' quarter, away from the tourist showrooms.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A slow afternoon and a spa treatment, or a return to the ghats to simply sit and watch.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A final rooftop dinner over the river before departure.

items.name: Assi Ghat
items.description: The quieter southern end near the university, calmer, with good cafés.

items.name: Dashashwamedh / central ghats
items.description: The spiritual heart where the aarti happens, intense and central.

items.name: Cantonment
items.description: Away from the ghats with the larger hotels, for comfort and quiet at night.

events.name: Dev Deepawali
events.note: The 'Diwali of the gods', every ghat lined with thousands of oil lamps on Kartik Purnima.

events.name: Ganga Mahotsav
events.note: A festival of classical music and culture on the riverbank, around Dev Deepawali.

events.name: Mahashivratri
events.note: The great night of Shiva fills the temples of his holiest city; date follows the lunar calendar.

onGround.heading: On the ground
onGround.note: A private boat at sunrise and the evening Ganga Aarti at Dashashwamedh Ghat are the two essentials, arrange both privately to avoid the crush. Dress modestly, remove shoes at temples, and be discreet with the camera around the cremation ghats, where photography is not welcome.

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Lal Bahadur Shastri Airport (VNS), about 45 minutes to an hour from the ghats, and take a chauffeured car; the Taj Nadesar Palace and BrijRama-style riverside properties will arrange the transfer, the last stretch sometimes by boat.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private car to the edge of the old city, then on foot through the lanes (which no car can enter) and by private boat along the Ganges at dawn and dusk.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: 4G works but can be congested near the ghats during festivals; a preloaded Jio or Airtel eSIM and hotel wifi keep you covered.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Indian rupee (INR); cards are fine at hotels but the old city runs on cash, so carry small notes, and tip boatmen and guides around 10 percent.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: November to February is the kind season: cool, dry, the ghats and river at their most serene, though January mornings bring fog. Avoid the fierce heat of May-June and the July-September monsoon, when the Ganga runs high.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Direct from Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru into Lal Bahadur Shastri Airport (VNS); Air India, IndiGo, Akasa and SpiceJet fly the routes, with Delhi and Bengaluru the busiest. A modern airport about 25km from the ghats, so allow for traffic and let the hotel arrange the transfer.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: Routine Hep A/typhoid cover advised; it is a dense, intense city. Safe but crowded, especially at the ghats, where a private guide and quiet timing help. Do not enter the river; sealed water only, and winter air can be poor.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Deeply easy; Varanasi is a temple city where pure-vegetarian and Jain food is the norm and satvik cooking is everywhere. The dining at BrijRama Palace and Taj Nadesar Palace is refined vegetarian; the local kachori-sabzi and chaat are vegetarian street classics.
